newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK legislature staff set to help replacement body.
newsitem.headline: HK legislature staff set to help replacement body.

text.p: Administrative staff from Hong Kong's Legislative Council on Tuesday were cleared to serve the controversial provisional body that will replace it after the British colony reverts to China this year.

The Legislative Council Commission, the body that oversees Hong Kong's lawmaking body, voted to allow members of its secretariat to serve the provisional legislature ahead of the July 1 handover, a move likely to incur the fury of pro-democracy legislators.

The staffers, expected to number about 15, would have to resign their positions, but they would be allowed shorter than required notice periods, retain their benefits, and may be allowed to rejoin the secretariat after the handover.
The 300-member secretariat provides administrative support and services to Legislative Council (Legco) members.
Legco president Andrew Wong, who heads the commission, said the move was aimed at smoothing the transition, although details of which staff may move were undecided.
"It was merely a decision in principle that we are prepared to engage in talks with the provisional legislative council on such arrangements," Wong told a news conference.
"The entire move is to ensure the smooth transition of the secretariat," he said.
The decision is likely to further polarise the 60-member chamber, about half of whom are also members of the provisional legislature.

The commission, made up of sitting legislators, voted four to three. Those in favour were all members of the new body and those against were pro-democracy stalwarts boycotting what they view to be an illegal replacement council, local media reported.
Britain and Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp have denounced the provisional legislature as a sham. The body was chosen in December by a 400-member pro-China panel.

Britain has also challenged China to go to the World Court to see if the body conforms with handover agreements, while the Democratic Party has branded the legislature illegal and a violation of handover treaties.
China plans to install the body in Hong Kong on July 1 and to dissolve Legco which was elected in 1995 for a four-year term.
The provisional legislature will hold its first formal session on January 25 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, a Beijing-controlled newspaper reported in Hong Kong on Tuesday.
